title: What To Do If You’re Attacked By A Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by an acquaintance's assault by an enraged student, Linsin lays out ten guidelines for teacher physical safety, ranging from never creating friction that could invite revenge violence, to always maintaining ten feet of distance from an escalating student, to having a concrete escape strategy planned in advance. He advises moving the rest of the class back and speaking to an agitated student from a safe distance rather than approaching, and offers specific instructions for the worst-case scenario of being physically attacked: closing the distance into a controlled bear hug is described as safer than being caught at striking range, and fighting back is endorsed as a last resort when escape and restraint both fail. He closes by criticizing a district policy that shields student attackers from law enforcement referral, urging teachers to call 911 and press charges if assaulted.
points: Never creating friction with students — no scolding, berating, or intimidation — is framed as reducing the risk of revenge violence.
Maintaining at least ten feet of distance from an agitated or aggressive student is repeated as the central safety guideline.
Teachers are advised to think through an escape strategy in advance: where to go, who to call, how to avoid being cornered.
In the worst case of being physically attacked and unable to escape, pulling the student into a controlled bear hug is described as safer than being at striking distance.
Fighting back is endorsed only as a last resort, solely to create space to escape, not to seek retaliation.
quotes: According to the NEA, six percent of teachers have been attacked by a student. That’s over 200,000 teachers.

One of our core tenets here at SCM is to never scold, berate, lecture, or otherwise create friction with students. Not only does this make classroom management more effective, but it goes a long way toward ensuring your safety.
Stay back ten feet or more, calmly guide the rest of your class to do the same, and talk to the student from there.
Striking distance—between one and three feet—is the absolute worst place you can be. Best, of course, is ten feet or more. However, if you can’t get away, then believe it or not, closer is safest .
Fight, kick, punch, push, scream, and run the second you have an opening. Do not seek your own revenge. Fight only insofar as to give yourself space to get away.
If you have been attacked or threatened with violence, I urge you to call 911 and insist on pressing charges. If not for you, then for the next teacher.
